analogy.p: A character set is like a phone book where every symbol is a name and its binary code is that person's phone number. To store the letter A, the computer looks A up and writes down its number, 65; to show the letter again it looks the number up in the same book. Everyone has to use the same edition of the book, otherwise a number could ring a different person and the wrong symbol appears. ASCII is a small local phone book that only lists 128 English-style names, while Unicode is a giant worldwide directory with room for every language and emoji, although the longer numbers take up more room on the page. The analogy breaks down because a phone number is normally just looked up once, whereas a computer must look up every single character each time it reads or writes text, and the 'numbers' themselves are fixed by agreement rather than chosen when someone signs up.

bullets: A character set is a **defined list of characters** that a computer can recognise, each matched to a **unique binary code**.
Characters include upper-case letters, lower-case letters, digits (0 to 9), punctuation, the space character and symbols.
The numbers in a character set are just labels: nothing about the number 65 is 'A-like'. It is a **convention** that everyone has agreed to follow.
Two main character sets are on the OCR J277 specification: **ASCII** and **Unicode**.
If two systems use different character sets, the same binary code can show different symbols, so text appears as **gibberish**.
Using a **standard** character set means files and messages can be shared between different computers, programs and countries.
core.p: A **character** is any single symbol you can type: a letter, a digit, a punctuation mark, a space or a symbol such as £ or @. Computers can only store **binary**, so every character has to be turned into a binary number before it can be stored or processed. A **character set** is the agreed list of characters a computer system can use, in which every character is given its own unique **binary code** (a number). When you press a key, the computer looks the character up in the character set and stores its code; when it needs to show the text, it does the reverse look-up. This only works if the sender and receiver use the same character set.

bullets: Computers use binary because transistors have **two states** (on = 1, off = 0).
The same bit pattern can be a **number, a character, part of an image or part of a sound**, depending on how the program interprets it.
Text is therefore stored as a **sequence of binary codes**, one code per character, in the order they are typed.
A word like 'cat' is three codes next to each other: one for c, one for a and one for t.
Spaces and line breaks are characters too and have their own codes, so they take up space in the file.
Text files stored this way are called **plain text**; word-processor files add extra data for fonts and formatting.
core.h: Why characters must be stored as binary
core.p: All data inside a computer, whether numbers, images, sound or text, is stored as **binary** (1s and 0s) because the electronic components in a processor and memory have two states: on and off. A letter has no natural binary form, so we need a rule that maps each character to a number, and then stores that number in binary. That rule is the character set. Without it, the bit pattern 01000001 could mean the number 65, part of a pixel colour or the letter A, and the computer would not know which. The **context** (the file type and the character set used) tells the computer how to interpret the bits.

bullets: Step 1: a key is pressed (for example the letter H).
Step 2: the character is looked up in the character set and found to have the code **72**.
Step 3: 72 is converted to binary: 64 + 8, so **1001000** in 7 bits.
Step 4: the bits are stored in memory or on disk, then the next character's code follows immediately after.
Displaying text is the same process **in reverse**: binary to code to character to pixels on screen.
Leading zeros matter: every character in a fixed-width set uses the **same number of bits**, so 33 is stored as 0100001, not 100001.
Because every code has the same length, a computer can find the 10th character simply by counting bits (10 x 7 bits along).
core.h: How a character is stored: step by step
core.p: The process of turning typed text into stored bits follows a fixed sequence. First the key is pressed and the keyboard sends a signal to the computer. The operating system looks the character up in the **character set** to find its numerical code in denary. That denary number is converted to **binary**, padded with leading zeros to the correct number of bits (7 for ASCII), and stored in memory. To display the character, the computer reads the binary, converts it back to the code, looks the code up in the character set and sends the matching shape to the screen using a font.

bullets: ASCII = American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
**7 bits** per character, so **128** characters (codes 0 to 127).
Codes 0 to 31 and 127 are **control codes** (non-printing), for example 10 = line feed (new line) and 9 = tab.
Codes 32 to 126 are **printable characters**; 32 is the space.
It has the 26 capital letters, 26 lower-case letters, 10 digits and a range of punctuation and symbols.
It does **not** contain accented letters (such as é), non-Latin alphabets (such as Arabic or Chinese) or emojis.
Computers store ASCII characters in 8-bit bytes in practice, with the extra leading bit set to 0, so one ASCII character normally takes one byte.
core.p: **ASCII** stands for the **American Standard Code for Information Interchange**. It was developed to give a standard way for different machines to share text. Standard ASCII uses **7 bits** per character, which gives 2^7 = **128** different codes, numbered 0 to 127. Those 128 codes cover the English alphabet in upper and lower case, the digits 0 to 9, punctuation marks and a set of non-printing control characters. ASCII is simple and very compact, which made it ideal for early computers with very little memory, but it can only handle English-style text.

bullets: **Lower case = capital + 32**, so 'a' = 97 and 'A' = 65 (97 - 65 = 32).
To find a letter's code from another: 'G' is 6 letters after 'A', so its code is 65 + 6 = **71**.
Space is **32**, which is lower than any letter or digit, so a space sorts before them.

Because 'B' (66) > 'A' (65), a program can check alphabetical order by comparing character codes; but capitals (65 to 90) are all less than lower-case (97 to 122), so 'Z' sorts before 'a' unless case is converted first.
core.h: Useful patterns in the ASCII table
core.p: You are not expected to memorise the whole table, but the **order** of the codes is carefully designed and is very useful. Digits, capital letters and lower-case letters each form a **continuous run** in alphabetical or numerical order. That means if you are given the code of one letter, you can work out the code of any other by counting along. The lower-case letters are exactly **32 higher** than the matching capitals. Because the letters are in order, comparing the codes of two letters tells the computer which comes first alphabetically, which is how sorting and searching text works.

bullets: Extended ASCII: **8 bits**, **256** characters (0 to 255).
The first 128 codes match standard ASCII, so older text still works.
Many **different versions** of the upper 128 codes existed, so text could display incorrectly when moved between systems.
256 codes can hold one alphabet comfortably but not several alphabets at once.
One extra bit **doubles** the number of characters available (each extra bit multiplies by 2).
Files in extended ASCII use **1 byte per character**, the same as standard ASCII stored in a byte.
core.p: Because computers work in 8-bit **bytes**, the extra eighth bit was soon used to double the number of characters. **Extended ASCII** uses **8 bits** per character, giving 2^8 = **256** codes (0 to 255). The first 128 codes are the same as standard ASCII, and the additional 128 codes were used for accented letters, currency symbols, box-drawing characters and so on. The problem was that different countries used the upper 128 codes for **different** symbols, so there were many incompatible versions. Even 256 characters is far too few for languages such as Chinese or Japanese, which have thousands of characters.

bullets: Number of characters = **2 to the power of the number of bits**: 2^n.
Adding **1 bit doubles** the number of characters (7 bits to 8 bits: 128 to 256).
To find bits needed: 2^6 = 64, 2^7 = 128, so a set of 100 characters needs **7 bits**; a set of 200 characters needs **8 bits**.
A fixed number of bits per character means every character takes the **same storage**.
More bits per character allows more characters **but** makes each stored character larger, so files get bigger.
Worked pattern: 'How many characters can 10 bits represent?' is 2^10 = 1024.
core.h: Bits per character and number of characters
core.p: The central calculation on this point is the relationship between the number of **bits** and the number of **different characters** that can be stored. With n bits there are 2^n different binary patterns, and each pattern can be given to a different character. So 7 bits give 2^7 = 128 patterns, 8 bits give 256, 16 bits give 65,536 and 32 bits give 4,294,967,296 (about 4.3 billion). **Every extra bit doubles** the number of characters that can be represented. If you are asked how many bits are needed for a set with a given number of characters, you find the smallest n where 2^n is at least that number.

bullets: ASCII's 128 characters cannot cover **non-English languages** or symbols.
Extended ASCII fixed some problems but created **many incompatible versions**.
The internet made it essential for people in different countries to read each other's text correctly.
Unicode provides **one universal standard** for all writing systems.
Unicode also includes **emojis**, mathematical symbols, currency symbols and historic scripts.
Websites and operating systems today overwhelmingly use Unicode, so text from any country displays correctly.
Examples of a reason to choose Unicode: a website with Chinese, Arabic and English text on the same page.
core.h: Why ASCII is not enough: the need for Unicode
core.p: ASCII was designed for English. With only 128 (or 256) characters it cannot represent the alphabets and writing systems used around the world, such as Arabic, Greek, Cyrillic, Hindi, Chinese, Japanese and Korean, nor mathematical symbols or emojis. Different countries created their own incompatible sets of 256 codes, which made sharing documents and websites unreliable. As the internet connected the whole world, a single universal standard was needed. **Unicode** was created to be that standard: one character set that gives every character in every language its own unique code.

bullets: Unicode uses **more bits per character** (commonly 16 or 32 bits in the specification wording) so it can store far more characters.
Each character has a unique **code point**; for example the code point for 'A' is still **65**.
The first 128 Unicode characters are the **same as ASCII**, so ASCII text is valid Unicode.
UTF-8 is variable length: English letters use **1 byte** but other characters use 2, 3 or 4 bytes.
Unicode includes **emojis**, accented letters, non-Latin alphabets, mathematical and technical symbols.
The standard is maintained by an organisation called the Unicode Consortium and new characters are added in new versions.
For GCSE you need to state that Unicode uses more bits and so can represent more characters; the details of UTF are an extension.
core.h: Unicode: what it is and how it works
core.p: **Unicode** is a character set that uses **more bits per character** than ASCII, so it can represent a very large number of characters: well over 100,000 are already defined, covering most of the world's writing systems, and there is room for many more. Each character has a unique number called a **code point**. Common Unicode encodings use 8, 16 or 32 bits (or a mixture): **UTF-8** uses between 1 and 4 bytes per character, **UTF-16** uses 2 or 4 bytes and **UTF-32** uses 4 bytes. Importantly, the first **128** Unicode code points are identical to ASCII, so Unicode is **backwards compatible** with ASCII.

bullets: **ASCII**: 7 bits, 128 characters, mostly English, small file size.
**Unicode**: more bits (e.g. 16 or 32), thousands of characters, all languages and emojis, bigger file size.
Both give each character a **unique binary code**.
The first 128 Unicode characters match ASCII, so Unicode can be seen as an **extension** of ASCII.
Unicode needs more storage and more bandwidth for the same number of characters: 100 characters is 700 bits in ASCII but 1,600 bits in 16-bit Unicode.
ASCII is suitable when only English text is needed and **memory is limited**; Unicode is suitable for **international** text.
Comparison phrase: 'Unicode can represent more characters **because** it uses more bits per character.'
core.p: Examiners often ask you to compare the two character sets. The core trade-off is **range against storage**. ASCII is compact because each character uses just 7 (or 8) bits, but it can only represent a small set of characters. Unicode uses more bits per character, so it can represent every language, but a text stored in 16-bit or 32-bit Unicode takes 2 to 4 times as much space as the same text in ASCII. To earn full marks, state a difference and a reason, and link the number of bits to the number of characters or the file size.

bullets: **Size in bits = number of characters x bits per character.**
Bytes = bits / 8; kilobytes = bytes / 1000; megabytes = kilobytes / 1000.
'Hello World!' has 12 characters (the space and ! count), so 12 x 7 = **84 bits** in 7-bit ASCII.
The same text in 8-bit extended ASCII is 12 x 8 = 96 bits = **12 bytes**.
In 16-bit Unicode it is 12 x 16 = 192 bits = **24 bytes**; in 32-bit Unicode, 48 bytes.
To compare: 16-bit Unicode is **twice** the size of 8-bit; 32-bit is four times the size of 8-bit.
Work in bits first, then convert once at the end, to avoid slips.
core.h: Calculating the size of a text file
core.p: File size questions are very common. For a text stored with a fixed number of bits per character, the size is simply the **number of characters multiplied by the number of bits per character**. Remember that spaces, punctuation and line breaks count as characters. Convert bits to bytes by dividing by 8, and bytes to kilobytes by dividing by 1000 (OCR uses 1 kilobyte = 1000 bytes). Always show the multiplication and give the unit, because the mark scheme gives method marks.

bullets: The digit character '5' has code **53**; the number five in binary is **101** (just the value).
Digit characters '0' to '9' have codes 48 to 57, so the value of a digit character = **code - 48**.
Comparing as text goes character by character from the left, so '10' < '9' because '1' (49) < '9' (57).
Phone numbers, postcodes and product codes are normally stored as **text** because you never do arithmetic on them and they may start with 0.
In OCR Exam Reference Language, **ASC(character)** returns the character's code and **CHR(number)** returns the character for a code.
Example: ASC('A') returns 65 and CHR(97) returns 'a'.
Casting input to int is needed before maths: the string '5' + '3' joins to '53' but integers 5 + 3 give 8.
core.p: A common confusion is between a **number** and the **character** for a digit. When you type the symbol 5 into a text box, it is stored as a character with ASCII code 53 (binary 0110101), not as the binary number 101. Only if a program converts the text to an integer is it stored as the number five. This is why programs have to convert (cast) typed input before doing arithmetic, and why 'sorting' numbers stored as text can give strange results such as '10' coming before '9'.

bullets: **Binary and hexadecimal**: ASCII codes are often shown in hex, for example 'A' is 41 in hex (65 in denary).
**Images and sound**: colour depth and bit depth follow the same 'bits give 2^n possibilities' rule.
**Compression**: text files can be compressed, for example by lossless methods like run-length encoding or dictionary methods.
**Programming**: strings are lists of characters; ASC() and CHR() convert between characters and codes.
**Databases and validation**: text fields store characters; length checks count characters.
**Networks**: web pages declare their character encoding (usually UTF-8) so browsers display text correctly.
**Storage units**: counting how many characters fit on a device uses bits, bytes and kilobytes.
core.p: Character representation links to many other parts of the course. It uses the **binary and denary conversion** skills from the data representation unit, and the idea of bits and bytes from storage. File sizes feed into **compression** and calculating storage needs, and the same pattern, 'more bits means more possibilities but a bigger file', also appears in image colour depth and sound bit depth. In programming, strings are sequences of characters, and string comparison, sorting and validation (such as checking a letter is upper case) all depend on character codes. In networks and security, text sent over the internet must be encoded and decoded using the same character set.

bullets: Lower to upper: new code = old code - 32. 'q' is 113, 113 - 32 = 81 = 'Q'.
Upper to lower: add 32.
In binary the only difference between 'A' (1000001) and 'a' (1100001) is the **32s bit**.
A Caesar shift of 3 turns 'A' (65) into 68, which is 'D'.
Wrapping: 'Y' (89) + 3 = 92, which is not a capital, so subtract 26 to get 66 = 'B'.
Checking whether a character is a capital: code is between 65 and 90 inclusive.
Checking whether a character is a digit: code is between 48 and 57 inclusive.
core.h: Higher-level extension: case conversion and Caesar shifts
core.p: Because the letters are in order, programmers can manipulate text using arithmetic on character codes. To convert a lower-case letter to a capital you subtract 32 from its code; in binary this just clears the bit with value 32. A Caesar cipher shifts each letter along the alphabet by adding a fixed number to its code and wrapping round after Z. These are not extra content you must learn, but they show why the ordering of codes matters and often appear as programming questions.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark)**: a short fact such as 'ASCII uses 7 bits per character' or 'Unicode can represent more characters'. One idea, no explanation needed.
**Describe how a character is stored (2 to 3 marks)**: each character is given a unique number/binary code in a character set; the code is converted to binary; the binary is stored in memory.

**Explain why Unicode was introduced (2 marks)**: ASCII only has 128 characters / cannot represent other languages (1); Unicode uses more bits per character so can represent many more characters/all languages (1).

**Compare ASCII and Unicode (up to 4 marks)**: a clear difference in bits per character (1), a difference in number of characters (1), a difference in file size/storage (1), and the similarity that both give each character a unique code or that the first 128 match (1).
**Calculation (2 to 3 marks)**: number of characters x bits per character (method), correct bits, then correct conversion to bytes if asked. Always show units.
**'How many bits are needed?' questions**: list powers of 2 (64, 128, 256 ...) and choose the smallest that is big enough. State the answer with the reasoning for the mark.
**Use command words**: 'State' means a fact only, 'Describe' means say what happens, 'Explain' needs a because/so link, and 'Compare' needs both sides in the same sentence or a clear 'whereas'.

**Model phrases**: 'a character set is a list of characters, each with a unique binary code'; 'more bits per character means more characters can be represented'; 'a larger file size because each character uses more bits'.
**ASCII code puzzles**: if given 'A = 65', work out other letters by counting along the alphabet; show the sum (for example 65 + 6 = 71) to earn the method mark.
**Six-mark discussion questions**: give a balanced answer: the benefits of Unicode (languages, emojis, compatibility), the cost (storage, bandwidth), and a conclusion about which suits the scenario.
**Avoid vague words**: 'bigger', 'better' and 'more modern' earn no marks without saying what is bigger (the file size), better at what (more characters) and why (more bits).

mistakes.r: Standard ASCII uses 7 bits and has 128 characters; extended ASCII uses 8 bits and has 256 characters.
mistakes.w: Saying ASCII has 256 characters (or 8 bits) without qualification.

mistakes.r: Unicode uses more bits per character, so it can represent more different characters, including other languages and emojis.
mistakes.w: Saying Unicode 'has more characters' with no reason given.

mistakes.r: The character '5' has ASCII code 53 (0110101); 101 is the binary number five.
mistakes.w: Saying the binary code for the character '5' is 101.

mistakes.r: The number of characters is 2 to the power of the number of bits: 2^7 = 128.
mistakes.w: Giving the number of characters as 7 x 2 (or 2 x 7) for 7 bits.

mistakes.r: Every character counts, including spaces, full stops and line breaks, each with its own code and bits.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to count spaces and punctuation when calculating the size of a text.

mistakes.r: Unicode normally uses more bits per character, so text files are larger than the same text in ASCII.
mistakes.w: Saying Unicode takes less storage because it is more modern.

mistakes.r: ASCII is a standard, so the same character has the same code on every system that uses it; that is its purpose.
mistakes.w: Writing that ASCII codes are different for different computers.

mistakes.r: They have different codes: A = 65 and a = 97, which differ by 32.
mistakes.w: Thinking lower-case 'a' has the same code as 'A'.

mistakes.r: Check the unit asked for: divide bits by 8 to get bytes, and show the units in your answer.
mistakes.w: Giving the answer in bytes when bits were asked (or the reverse).

summary: You must know that computers store text by giving every character a unique binary code from a character set, and be able to describe ASCII (7 bits, 128 characters) and Unicode (more bits per character, so many more characters including other languages and emojis). You must link the number of bits per character to the number of characters available, and use this to explain why Unicode was introduced and why it makes text files bigger. It matters because every piece of text on a computer, from this page to a password, is stored this way.

terms.d: A single symbol that can be entered or displayed, such as a letter, digit, punctuation mark, space or symbol.
The defined list of characters a computer system can recognise, each with a unique binary code.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a character set that uses 7 bits per character to represent 128 characters.
An 8-bit version of ASCII with 256 codes; the first 128 match standard ASCII.
A character set that uses more bits per character than ASCII so it can represent characters from all the world's languages and symbols such as emojis.
The unique number given to a character in the Unicode character set.
A binary digit: a single 1 or 0, the smallest unit of data.
A non-printing character code that controls the device or layout, such as a new line or tab.
The pattern of 1s and 0s used to represent a character (or other data) in a computer.
A Unicode encoding that uses a variable number of bytes (1 to 4) per character; the first 128 characters are the same as ASCII.
The process of converting characters into binary codes using a character set.
Converting stored binary codes back into characters using the character set.
A file containing only characters from a character set with no formatting data.
A sequence of characters treated as one piece of data in a program.

worked.q: A text message contains 40 characters, including spaces. It is stored using 7-bit ASCII. Calculate the size of the message in bits and in bytes (to 1 decimal place). [3 marks]
steps: Size in bits = number of characters x bits per character.
40 x 7 = 280 bits. (1 mark for method, 1 for answer in bits)
Check: 35 x 8 = 280, so the conversion is correct.

worked.q: The ASCII code for the capital letter 'A' is 65. (a) State the code for 'F'. (b) Write the code for 'F' in 7-bit binary. (c) State the code for 'f'. [4 marks]
steps: F is 5 letters after A (B, C, D, E, F), so the code is 65 + 5 = 70.
Convert 70 to binary: 64 + 4 + 2 = 70, so the 64, 4 and 2 columns are 1: 1000110 (7 bits).
Check: 102 = 64 + 32 + 4 + 2 = 1100110 and 'f' is the 6th letter after 'a' (97 + 5 = 102).

worked.ans: Model answer: ASCII uses only 7 bits, so it can represent just 128 characters and has no Japanese characters. Unicode uses more bits per character, so it can represent characters from many languages, letting the website show both English and Japanese correctly. A disadvantage is that Unicode uses more bits per character, so text files are larger, using more storage and taking longer to download.
worked.q: A company's website is used by customers in the UK and in Japan. Explain why the company should use Unicode rather than 7-bit ASCII for its web pages. Include one disadvantage of Unicode. [4 marks]
steps: Point 1: 7-bit ASCII only has 128 characters and cannot represent Japanese characters.
Point 2: Unicode uses more bits per character, so can represent many more characters, including Japanese and English together.
Point 3: the first 128 Unicode characters match ASCII, so the English text will still display correctly.
Disadvantage: each character takes more bits, so the files are larger and use more storage and bandwidth.
